title: Evan Williams on the Louisville wharf
summary: Welsh immigrant Evan Williams distilled corn whiskey on Louisville’s Ohio River bank by 1801 and served as the town’s first wharf master.
bodyMarkdown:
Evan Williams was a Welsh immigrant who became one of early Louisville's best-known whiskey makers. He [was born in Dale, Pembrokeshire](https://grokipedia.com/page/Evan_Williams_%28bourbon%29). Today his name is on one of the best-selling bourbons in the world, but historians still debate how much of his traditional story is true.

## The traditional story

In the version told on bottle labels and markers, Williams settled in Louisville and began distilling there in 1783. [Grokipedia's Evan Williams article](https://grokipedia.com/page/Evan_Williams_%28bourbon%29) says he was born in 1755 and came to Louisville around 1780. It describes his 1783 distillery on the bank of the Ohio River as Kentucky's first commercial distillery. A historical marker in Louisville makes the same claim.

Grokipedia says Williams made whiskey from local corn surpluses and shipped it by flatboat down the Ohio. By 1801, federal records show he ran three stills holding 141, 130 and 93 gallons, and that year he got a federal distilling license.

## A busy townsman

Williams was more than a distiller. Grokipedia calls him a master stonemason who worked on Jefferson County's first jail and courthouse. He was also one of Louisville's elected town trustees.

In 1797 he was elected Louisville's first wharf master. In that role he oversaw activity along the riverfront and worked on sanitation there. His own business drew legal trouble over distillery sanitation in 1788 and 1802. Grokipedia says he kept distilling until his death in Louisville on October 15, 1810.

## What the records show

The 1783 date is disputed. Historian Michael Veach of the Filson Historical Society says the claim that Williams was Kentucky's first distiller did not appear until an 1892 publication by Reuben Durrett, more than a century later. Veach also points to a record of Williams traveling from London to Philadelphia in May 1794. If that record is right, Williams could only have started his distillery well after 1783, not in the year the brand celebrates.

Veach argues that Kentucky's first distiller may never be known, because records from the period are poor. Better candidates, he says, include Jacob Myers and the brothers Joseph and Samuel Davis, who reportedly arrived in 1779. Other early Kentucky whiskey makers, such as [Jacob Spears](/stories/jacob-spears-early-bourbon-whiskey/), have their own stories.

## The modern brand

Heaven Hill introduced the Evan Williams brand in 1957. Grokipedia notes that the company has no family or business link to Williams's original distillery and chose the name as a tribute. The black label still reads "Since 1783" and "Kentucky's 1st distiller."

The bourbon is distilled at Heaven Hill's Bernheim Distillery in Louisville and bottled in Bardstown. Heaven Hill was founded in 1935 and is still run by the Shapira family.

## Kentucky today

The Evan Williams Bourbon Experience on Louisville's Whiskey Row tells the brand's story. It is part of the Kentucky Bourbon Trail. Visitors can see where the legend is set, but the history behind it remains open to question.
